title: Interior Antarctica is undergoing marked climate change
abstract: 2024 is the warmest year in NASA’s 145-year climate record. Unlike the Arctic, which has experienced significantly faster warming than the global average, Antarctic temperature change is variable. Here we employ our observational reconstruction to show that although Antarctica has experienced warming on average, the long-term temperature trends exhibit notable spatial structure and reveal major disparities with CMIP6 models. Specifically, long-term observed warming is found in the Antarctic Peninsula and West Antarctica, with modest cooling in parts of East Antarctica, particularly during austral autumn and winter. CMIP6 substantially overestimates the Antarctic warming similar to the global rate and maximizes over the Antarctic interior. However, average and extreme temperature observations demonstrate that interior Antarctica is experiencing marked climate change, paralleling the projected CMIP6 behavior but with reduced magnitude. Elsewhere climate change is happening in the northern Antarctic Peninsula and coastal West Antarctica but is muted along the East Antarctic coast. Interior Antarctica is nearing major climate change while the northern Antarctic Peninsula and coastal West Antarctica are already experiencing it, according to observational reconstructions and model simulations.
problem: Current climate models (CMIP6) substantially overestimate the magnitude of Antarctic warming and fail to replicate observed regional and seasonal temperature variations, such as cooling in East Antarctica, when compared to observational reconstructions.
method: This study analyzes Antarctic climate change by comparing an updated observational temperature reconstruction (RECON) against CMIP6 models and ERA5 reanalysis data to assess spatial, seasonal, and extreme temperature trends, both with and without the influence of the Southern Annular Mode.
task: The task is to investigate spatial and seasonal climate change in Antarctica by comparing an observational temperature reconstruction with CMIP6 climate models to analyze long-term temperature trends, disparities between observations and models, and the escalation of extreme weather events.
innovation: By comparing observational reconstruction with CMIP6 models, this paper demonstrates that interior Antarctica is undergoing marked climate change, revealing that models correctly project the warming pattern but substantially overestimate its magnitude and fail to capture key regional trends.

The AP region showed the strongest positive trend during the autumn, followed by spring and winter, potentially linked to positive SAM phases and increased occurrences of atmospheric river activity24.
In contrast, along coastal EA between 60° and 180°E, a negative trend was observed during all seasons except spring.
Furthermore, Marie Byrd Land also indicated a negative trend for all seasons except winter.

Further, the extreme warming trend over eastern Dronning Maud Land primarily in spring and somewhat in summer in ERA5 (Fig. 7) coincides with the warming in that region reported by Kurita et al.10 which occurs between October and March.
These results suggest that extreme warmth is becoming more frequent across most of interior East Antarctica, as shown by ERA5.

While RECON highlights notable variations in the Antarctic SAT trend, emphasizing a long-term cooling in EA during autumn and minimal warming in winter, as well as a marked warming trend in WA during winter and spring, these patterns are not replicated in the CMIP6 MMM that shows amplified interior warming during all seasons.
